name: Findchóem
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Findchóem, known also as Finncháem or Fionnchaomh, is a heroine or goddess of Ireland. Like other women in Irish myth, she sought an odd path to pregnancy. Finding a worm floating in a glass of holy well water, she drank it whole, worm included, hoping to bear a hero. She gave birth to the hero Conall Cernach, yet her foster son Cúchulainn proved the stronger of the two. This manner of conception turns up beyond Ireland, such as tales of the founding mothers of Chinese ruling lines, and it may mark an era when family descent passed through the mother. Early Irish sources show such matriliny, with kings who carry their mothers' names. Ailill mac Máta, king of Connacht, took his name from his mother Máta, and Concobar Mac Nessa, whom Ulster crowned king, took his name from his mother, Nessa, and Nessa was Findchóem's mother as well. Findchóem may herself mirror her own mother, who bore a child in the very same manner.

Ailill mac Máta and Concobar Mac Nessa were kings named for their mothers, evidence of matriliny.
